strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: robust visual navigation with vision-language-action models, using 360-degree multi-view perception and sim-to-real transfer.
The system design is clear and well integrated: multi-view observation encoding with SigLIP, a Qwen2-7B LLM backbone, continuous velocity action head, and ~7 Hz inference speed.
The multi-expert RL teacher pipeline with privileged depth information and iterative teacher-student DAgger-style fine-tuning is reasonable and well motivated.
The capability-balanced data aggregation strategy is a sensible contribution for preventing the student from overfitting to easier capabilities and underfitting harder ones.
Simulation experiments cover reaching, squeezing, avoiding, and mixed scenes, and include useful ablations on balanced vs. unbalanced data and multi-expert vs. single-expert training.

Real-world deployment on a Unitree GO2 with four fisheye cameras qualitatively demonstrates promising behaviors such as narrow-corridor traversal, thin-obstacle avoidance, and dynamic obstacle handling.
weaknesses: The paper does not compare against recent VLA-based navigation methods such as NaVid, Uni-NaVid, TrackVLA, NavGPT, or other language-conditioned navigation policies, despite positioning itself as a VLA navigation model. The baselines (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) are not VLA methods and do not directly test the claimed benefits of VLA.

Real-world evaluation is entirely qualitative. There are no quantitative real-world success rates, collision rates, or comparisons to baselines, so the core claim of robust sim-to-real transfer is not rigorously supported.

The central claim that 360-degree multi-view perception is important is not isolated experimentally. There is no ablation comparing four views against one view, front-only view, or other camera configurations using the same VLA architecture.

The capability-balanced data aggregation is a heuristic based on weighted travel time. It is only compared with an unbalanced baseline, without comparisons to standard DAgger, uniform data mixing, or alternative weighting schemes, and sensitivity to alpha/epsilon is not analyzed.

The claim that the student VLA outperforms RL teachers is somewhat overstated: in Table II, the mixed VLA achieves squeezing success rate 71 versus 73 for the specialized squeezing RL expert, so improvements are not uniform across capabilities.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or dataset release is mentioned, and details of the VLA fine-tuning procedure (full fine-tuning vs. LoRA, exact tokenization, training schedule, data filtering) are insufficient for reproduction.

The technical novelty is moderate: multi-view VLA, teacher-student distillation, and DAgger-style online fine-tuning are existing ideas; the main new component is the capability-balanced data weighting, which is relatively simple and not extensively validated.
There is no limitations or societal-impact discussion, which is important for a safety-critical navigation system deployed on real robots.
Generalization is demonstrated only on one robot platform, one simulator, and custom scenes; it is unclear whether the approach transfers to other embodiments, datasets, or real-world distributions.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and well-motivated system, MM-Nav, that combines a multi-view (360°, four-camera) VLA model with a teacher–student distillation pipeline from three capability-specific RL experts (reaching, squeezing, avoiding). The combination is sensible and addresses a real limitation of prior single-view navigation policies.

The capability-balanced data aggregation scheme is a simple but effective mechanism. Using weighted travel time (WTT) to define per-capability performance gaps and re-weighting the online-collected expert data is intuitive and supported by the ablation in Fig. 6, where the balanced variant converges faster and more stably than the unbalanced one.

Quantitative simulation results in Table I are strong and consistent: the method attains the highest success rate, lowest collision rate, and shortest WTT across nearly all scenes (e.g., 71% SR in Squeezing vs. 18% for NavDP; 68% vs. 27% in Avoiding). The margins over iPlanner/ViPlanner/NavDP are substantial and not marginal.

The finding that the student VLA can surpass its RL teachers (Table II, Fig. 4, Fig. 6) is a genuinely interesting empirical result and is plausibly explained by the complementary nature of the three capabilities. This supports the core claim about the synergistic effect of multi-expert learning.

The continuous omnidirectional velocity output (vx, vy, vyaw) is a practical advantage over discrete-action VLA baselines, and the reported ~7 Hz inference with a 7B LLM is a reasonable operating point for real deployment.

Real-world experiments on a Unitree GO2 are qualitatively compelling, particularly the thin-rope avoidance (which LiDAR-based systems reportedly miss) and navigation around glass walls. These stress-test sim-to-real transfer in ways standard benchmarks do not.
The paper is generally clear and readable; the pipeline figure (Fig. 2) and training-strategy figure (Fig. 3) communicate the two-stage process effectively.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison (Table I) does not include any VLA-based navigation baselines (e.g., NaVid, Uni-NaVid, TrackVLA), which are the closest related work and are explicitly discussed in Related Work. Since the central claim is that a VLA model with multi-view input and multi-expert distillation outperforms prior approaches, the absence of direct VLA comparisons weakens the evidence for the core claim. Table II compares only the authors' own RL and VLA variants.

Real-world evaluation is entirely qualitative. The paper states that four real-world scenes were constructed to test sim-to-real transfer and generalization, but no success rates, collision rates, or trial counts are reported. Given that robust real-world transfer is a headline claim, quantitative real-world evidence is expected.

No limitations section or failure-case analysis is provided. The Mixed scene results (47% SR, 26% CR) are notably weaker than the individual scenes, indicating non-trivial generalization limits that are not discussed. There is also no societal-impact or safety discussion for a robot navigation system deployed near humans.

Novelty is somewhat incremental. Multi-view/surround-view perception, VLA-based navigation, teacher–student distillation from RL experts, and capability balancing are each individually established ideas; the contribution is primarily the specific combination and the online capability-balanced aggregation. The paper does not deeply analyze why the student outperforms the teacher beyond a qualitative explanation.

Several implementation details are underspecified, which hurts reproducibility: the exact action head architecture and how the action MSE loss and VQA loss are jointly trained are only briefly described; the VQA dataset subset [54] and its role in the navigation policy are not fully justified; the mapping from capability gaps to data proportions (Eqs. 5–6) involves hyperparameters (ε=0.1, α=0.3) whose sensitivity is not studied.

The baseline configurations (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) are described as being set up 'following its original setup,' but it is not clear whether these methods were adapted to receive the same four-camera input or run in a fair single-view regime, which affects the interpretation of the large margins.

The paper appears to be in a compact format that may not match ECCV's expected length and structure, and the RL expert training details (reward shaping, per-expert coefficients) are provided but the effect of these coefficients on final VLA performance is not ablated.

strengths: The problem is relevant and hard: visual-only navigation with 360-degree perception and direct sim-to-real transfer. The system is actually deployed on a Unitree GO2 with four fisheye cameras, and the qualitative demonstrations (avoiding thin fabric ropes that defeat the robot's LiDAR, squeezing between cluttered/transparent objects, handling a wheelchair pushed into its path) are non-trivial and visually convincing.

The teacher-student pipeline is sensible and well-motivated: three capability-specific RL experts trained with privileged depth are distilled into a single VLA student that outputs continuous velocity commands, and the reported ~7 Hz inference with a 7B LLM is practical for real deployment.

The capability-balanced data aggregation based on the weighted-travel-time gap (Eqs. 5-6) is a simple, clearly described mechanism, and Fig. 6 provides an internally controlled ablation showing the balanced variant reaches expert-level performance within 1-2 online iterations while the unbalanced variant lags, most clearly in squeezing and avoiding.

Table II is a useful controlled experiment: VLAs trained with the same total data budget but drawn from a single expert versus mixed experts show that mixing data yields cross-capability generalization (Mixed-VLA 80/71/68 vs. e.g. Squeezing-VLA 44/64/28), which supports the 'synergy' claim within the proposed framework.

Simulation results (Table I) show large margins over three navigation baselines in success rate, collision rate, and weighted travel time across reaching, squeezing, avoiding, and mixed scenes, with a plausible qualitative failure analysis for the single-front-view baselines.

Implementation detail is reasonably forthcoming (PPO with 128 parallel environments, reward coefficients for each capability, 500k initial expert steps plus 200k per iteration, camera height/FOV randomization), which helps reproducibility of the RL side.
weaknesses: The headline claim, that multi-view 360-degree perception is what enables robustness, is never ablated. There is no single-view variant of MM-Nav, no ablation on the number of cameras, and no control for the tokenization/history design. Comparisons against single-view baselines (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) are confounded by training data, architecture, action space, and the task-specific RL teacher data, so they cannot substantiate the 'Multi-View' contribution.

No VLA navigation model is actually compared against, despite the paper positioning itself extensively against NaVid, Uni-NaVid, NaVILA, TrackVLA, and similar work. The baselines are small or zero-shot planners, so the central question of whether MM-Nav is a better VLA navigator than existing VLAs is left untested. The related-work claim that VLA models are 'constrained by a discrete action space' is also inaccurate given existing continuous-action VLA policies.

The real-world experiments, described in the abstract as 'extensive', are reported only qualitatively. There are no success rates, trial counts, distance/time termination criteria, or repeated-run statistics for the four real scenes; Fig. 5 shows two anecdotal cases. The principal sim-to-real claim is therefore not quantitatively supported.

The 'student outperforms the teacher' result is surprising and unexplained. The RL experts reach only 65%/73%/58% success in the very capability scenes they specialize in, while the VLA student trained on their data reaches 80/71/68. No analysis (e.g., robustness to appearance, depth noise, memory, or scene shift) explains why an imitation student exceeds privileged-depth teachers, and no explanation is given for the teachers' low in-distribution success. This raises the possibility that the teachers were under-trained or evaluated in shifted scenes, which would confound the claim.

Statistical rigor is thin: 100 episodes per scene with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple training seeds, so method differences (e.g., 80 vs. 69 success in reaching) are not shown to be significant. It is also not stated whether baselines were retrained or fine-tuned on these scenes or evaluated zero-shot, and baseline checkpoints are unspecified, which undermines reproducibility and fairness of Table I.

Component ablations are largely missing beyond the data-balancing study: there is no ablation of privileged-depth distillation, of history length/sliding window k, of the coarse/fine tokenization, of the LLM size or the action head, or of the VQA auxiliary loss. It is therefore unclear how much of the gain comes from the VLA design versus the data-collection recipe.

There is an internal inconsistency in the efficiency claim: the text states the visual token sequence is kept to '192 tokens', but 4 coarse tokens per history frame over 7 frames plus 16 fine tokens for the current frame totals roughly 44, making the 7 Hz claim difficult to verify from the description.

Novelty is incremental. Multi-view VLAs, privileged-teacher distillation, DAgger-style online aggregation, and capability-specific experts are all established; the only genuinely new element is the WTT-gap-based data ratio heuristic, whose two hyperparameters (epsilon, alpha) are not ablated or sensitivity-tested.

Real-to-sim mismatch is unaddressed: the simulation robot is a 0.7 x 0.35 x 0.5 m cuboid while the real platform is a GO2 with different geometry and camera placement, and the fisheye undistortion/calibration pipeline and its effect on the policy are not described.

The paper contains no limitations discussion, no systematic failure analysis, and no discussion of safety or societal implications for a legged robot operating in human-populated, dynamic environments; no code or data release is mentioned, and the manuscript is formatted for an IEEE robotics venue rather than the target conference, with several figures (Figs. 1, 4, 6) too small to read reliably.

strengths: Presents a complete multi-view VLA navigation system that combines 360° RGB perception, continuous velocity control, and a 7B VLM backbone, with real-world deployment on a Unitree GO2 at approximately 7 Hz.
Introduces a practical multi-expert distillation pipeline with three capability-specific RL experts (reaching, squeezing, avoiding) and an iterative DAgger-style student-teacher training procedure.
Proposes a capability-balanced data aggregation scheme based on weighted travel time gap, with ablations showing faster and more stable improvement than unbalanced sampling.
Reports strong results on the InternVLA-N1 S1 point-goal benchmark (88.1% average SR), and custom IsaacLab benchmarks with SR, CR, and WTT metrics.
Includes extensive ablations: VQA co-training, multi-view vs. single-view, iterative refinement, balancing, expert combination, and latent-space visualization for sim-to-real alignment.
Provides detailed implementation and training hyperparameters, RL environment specifications, and deployment setup, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Inconsistent dataset scale claims: the abstract states 1.5M expert demonstrations and 300k VQA data, while the method/implementation uses 500k initial expert steps, 200k per iteration, 100k initial VQA data, and 40k VQA per iteration; these numbers do not reconcile with the reported four iterations.

Several overclaims: the stated 'more than 20% performance drop' without VQA is not supported by Table 1, and 'student VLA outperforms the RL teachers' is not true for squeezing (71 vs. 73 in Table 3).

Real-world evaluation lacks quantitative comparison to baseline navigation methods; it reports only a VQA ablation with 20 trials per scenario, without collision/safety metrics or confidence intervals.
Missing comparison to recent VLA navigation baselines (e.g., NaVid, Uni-NaVid, TrackVLA) on the public benchmark and in custom/real-world settings, despite discussing them in related work.

Potential fairness issue on InternVLA-N1: the main multi-view result uses 360° cameras while most prior baselines use front-view only; the single-view variant is reported but multi-view SOTA is still foregrounded without fully disentangling view count from method gains.
Deployment relies on an external RTX 5090 server and wireless communication; onboard feasibility, latency robustness, and safety/failure modes are not analyzed.
No code/data release or working project URL is provided, limiting reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameters.

The capability-balancing ablation compares only against a fixed unbalanced baseline; alternative sampling/weighting strategies are not tested, and the WTT metric's behavior under very low success rates is not discussed.

Multi-view fusion is under-specified: token organization across four cameras is described, but there is no ablation on number/placement of cameras, calibration sensitivity, or cross-view attention design.

strengths: Presents MM-Nav, a 7B multi-view VLA navigation policy that directly predicts continuous omnidirectional velocity from 360° RGB observations and achieves ~7 Hz inference, with real-world deployment on a Unitree GO2 robot.

Introduces a multi-expert RL data-generation pipeline for reaching, squeezing, and avoiding, trained with privileged depth information in tailored IsaacLab scenes, providing diverse and otherwise difficult-to-collect supervision for visual navigation.

Develops a capability-balanced iterative teacher-student refinement strategy that dynamically reweights data across capabilities based on weighted travel time gaps, effectively mitigating policy-distribution shift and capability imbalance during distillation.

Reports strong results on the public InternVLA-N1 System-1 point-goal navigation benchmark: 88.1% average success rate (86.3 Home / 89.9 Commercial) and competitive SPL, outperforming prior RGB and depth-based baselines.

Provides extensive ablations, including VQA co-training, multi-view vs. single-view observations, online iteration gains, capability-balanced data aggregation, and expert combination, with latent-space analysis supporting improved sim-to-real alignment.

Includes detailed implementation and appendix material covering RL expert environments, reward design, hyperparameters, and training setup, which substantially aids technical understanding and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation is primarily qualitative and includes only a small VQA ablation with 20 trials per scenario; it lacks quantitative comparison against competing navigation policies in real-world settings, which limits the strength of the sim-to-real claim.

The online teacher-student iteration relies on RL expert actions without clearly filtering or validating teacher reliability during aggregation; noisy teacher labels could affect robustness, and the paper does not analyze this failure mode.

Reproducibility is partially limited: no code or dataset release is indicated, the project page URL is omitted, and the custom simulation scenes/VQA subset details are not fully specified for external reproduction.

The VQA co-training uses general video QA data rather than navigation-specific data; while ablations show benefits, the mechanism is not fully disentangled from generic visual representation alignment, and navigation-centric VQA ablations would clarify the source of improvement.

The main benchmark comparison is not entirely apples-to-apples because prior baselines are front-view-only while MM-Nav uses four cameras; the single-view variant partly addresses this, but the multi-view advantage is demonstrated mainly through internal ablation rather than against matched multi-view baselines.
The paper does not include an explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion, which would be valuable given real-world robot deployment and potential safety, privacy, and security considerations.

strengths: The paper presents a complete end-to-end system: a 7B multi-view VLA policy consuming 360° surround-view RGB, outputting continuous omnidirectional velocity, and actually deployed on a Unitree GO2 at ~7 Hz. This is a non-trivial engineering integration with real hardware validation.

The multi-capability expert design (reaching, squeezing, avoiding) trained with privileged depth in tailored IsaacLab scenes, distilled into a VLA student via iterative DAgger-style aggregation, is a sensible recipe for acquiring rare/hazardous navigation skills (thin-obstacle avoidance, squeezing through clutter) that are hard to collect in the real world.

Real-world qualitative results cover genuinely challenging settings: thin suspended wires, cluttered corridor with transparent/glass walls, pedestrian avoidance, and a nighttime outdoor alley with unseen obstacles. Zero-shot sim-to-real demonstrations of this kind are valuable and not commonly reported.

The ablation suite is reasonably broad for a systems paper: VQA co-training on/off (Table 1, Fig. 5b), single- vs. multi-view (Table 1), balanced vs. unbalanced data aggregation (Fig. 7), and single- vs. mixed-expert training (Table 3). The UMAP/gap-axis latent analysis (Fig. 6) linking VQA co-training to reduced sim-to-real domain gap is an informative diagnostic.

The appendix is thorough (RL hyperparameters, reward decomposition in Table 4, PPO settings in Tables 5-6, training curves in Fig. 9), and the reported InternVLA-N1 S1 numbers (86.3/89.9 multi-view; 79.9/86.7 single-view) are strong relative to the listed baselines.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty for ECCV. Nearly every ingredient is established prior art: RL-teacher to VLA-student distillation (X-Nav, COMPASS), DAgger-style iterative aggregation (Ross et al.), VQA/video co-training to close the sim-to-real gap (TrackVLA/Uni-NaVid-style), surround-view input (cited [19]), and continuous velocity heads. The only genuinely new component, the capability-balanced ratio p_Cap ∝ g_Cap^α (Eqs. 5-6), is a simple heuristic reweighting whose evaluation (one balanced vs. one unbalanced run, Fig. 7) is thin.

The headline claim is framed favorably and only partially supported. 'Outperforming the best previous method (72.2%) by +15.9 points' compares an average over the two splits (86.3/89.9) against the best baseline's per-split values (63.2 Home / 81.2 Commercial), and the abstract reports the multi-view variant, which has an input-modality advantage over the front-view baselines. Table 1's caption says a single-view variant is reported 'for fair comparison', yet the highlighted/headline row is multi-view. More importantly, the most relevant VLA baselines (NaVid, Uni-NaVid) are cited but never evaluated, so the state-of-the-art claim is not fully established.

Internal inconsistencies in the data budget undermine reproducibility: the abstract claims '1.5 million expert demonstrations' and '300k real-world VQA data', whereas Sec. 3.4/3.5 state the initial dataset contains '500k steps from three RL experts' and '100k VQA data', with 40k VQA per iteration. The actual training-set size and composition are therefore unclear.

Real-world evidence is thin and uncontrolled: only four scenarios with 20 trials each, and the sole comparison is VQA vs. no-VQA. There is no real-world comparison against any baseline policy or against the RL experts, no variance/confidence intervals, and no per-trial protocol details. This does not substantiate the abstract's claim of 'extensive real-world experiments'.

Overclaiming relative to the presented results. The abstract/body assert the student 'outperforms the RL teachers', but Table 3 shows the VLA (Mixed-VLA) underperforming the squeezing RL expert (71 vs. 73 SR) and the comparison is confounded: the VLA benefits from aggregated multi-expert data, real-world VQA co-training, and RGB multi-view input, while the RL experts see privileged depth and are evaluated in-domain. The RL expert also fails badly on InternVLA-N1 (the paper's own note), so the teacher/student comparison is not on equal footing.

The 'Mixed' out-of-distribution scene is weakened by construction: the squeezing difficulty is 'intentionally reduced to keep the overall evaluation reasonable' and materials are altered. This undercuts the generalization claim, and the rationale for the chosen difficulty level is not justified or ablated.

The InternVLA-N1 comparison is not clearly controlled for action space (continuous omnidirectional velocity vs. the baselines' native action spaces) or observation (360° vs. front view), and it is not stated whether baselines were re-run under identical conditions. With only single runs of 100 episodes and no significance testing, several Table 1/Table 2 gaps are hard to interpret.

No failure analysis, limitations, or safety discussion despite claims of 'robust' and 'safe' navigation with physical deployment. The 7B model runs off-board and receives velocity requests over a network link, raising latency/robustness questions (and dependence on accurate global localization for the (x, y) goal prompt) that are never addressed. Minor issues also appear, e.g., the 'QA data' typo in Fig. 5, the unusual WTT definition (successful-episode time divided by SR), and the confusing Table 1 caption relative to the highlighted row.
